tagline.text: Pampanga's giant parols light up the night at San Fernando's Christmas festival

location.label: Location
location.text: Robinsons Starmills, San Fernando City, Pampanga (near the NLEX San Fernando exit)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Mid-December to early January (the competition is around the second Saturday of December)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱450–1,300 (day trip from Manila, per person)

children.text: The Giant Lantern Festival (Ligligan Parul) is a Christmas event in which the barangays of San Fernando City, Pampanga, build enormous star-shaped parols several meters across and compete in a light show. After the mid-December competition, the lanterns stay on exhibit until January 1, and watching is free. It can be done as a day trip from Manila via NLEX.

The Ligligan Parul is a giant parol competition held every December in San Fernando City, Pampanga. San Fernando is nicknamed the "Christmas Capital of the Philippines," and this festival is the heart of that title. Several barangays in the city each bring a big star-shaped lantern, and in 2025 ten barangays took part. The draw is the way lights and rotating devices switch thousands of bulbs on and off to the music, creating kaleidoscope-like patterns.

Its roots lie in the small paper lanterns carried in the nine-day lubenas prayer processions before the Simbang Gabi dawn Masses of Christmas. Sources differ on when it began: some say 1904 and others 1908. Wikipedia says the first electric parol event, with bulbs, was held in 1931, but this comes from a single source, so treat it as "reportedly." The festival could not be held in 1978–1979 under martial law, and in 2020, during COVID-19, only an exhibition was held without a competition. In 2017 a limit of 10,000 bulbs per parol was set, and in 2024 a rule requiring at least 30% LED materials was introduced, along with the first all-LED, rotor-operated parol.

Sources also describe the size of the parols differently. In 2025 local media (SunStar Pampanga) put the height at 10–12 feet, while the Philippine Star described about 6 m (20 feet), up to 1 tonne in weight, up to 1 million pesos to build, and about 3 months of work by a team of 20. Either way, the structures are far taller than a person, and both agree that thousands of bulbs are involved. Rules change from year to year, so it is better to remember simply that they are "very big" than to rely on exact numbers.

In recent years the venue has been the open ground in front of the Robinsons Starmills mall. It sits right beside the NLEX San Fernando exit, so it is easy to reach from Manila and close to Clark. The competition night draws crowds while the exhibition period is much quieter, so pick your day accordingly. The venue has moved several times: according to Wikipedia it was Paskuhan Village in 1990–1998, the Bren Z. Guiao Convention Center in 1999, SM City Pampanga in 2000–2007, and Robinsons Starmills from 2008. Older blogs and videos may therefore list a different location from today's.

The parol of each barangay takes the stage in turn, switching its lights on and off to the music. The highlight is the moment the rotors turn and the patterns keep shifting like a kaleidoscope. The 2025 competition was held on the night of Saturday, December 13, and it usually starts after sunset. The 2025 winner was Barangay Bulaon, which received a revolving trophy and a ₱300,000 cash prize, followed by Sto. Niño, Dolores and Calulut.

A rotor, made of a steel drum wound with wiring, sets the timing of the lights. Bulaon, the 2025 winner, is said to have fielded a team of a rotor maker, electricians and 15 rotor operators. Watching the people working behind the parol doubles the fun.

Even among star shapes, the colors and structures differ from barangay to barangay. In 2025 an 18-year-old maker built the parol for Barangay Calulut, which drew attention. New techniques appear every year, and many fans come back to see them. The winning barangay changes too: San Juan in 2022, Telabastagan in 2023, San Nicolas in 2024 (its first title in 24 years) and Bulaon in 2025.

San Fernando is known across the Philippines as the "Christmas Capital." Even after the competition ends, the parols stay on display throughout December, and the city is full of Christmas decorations, making it a great place to enjoy the festive season.

In 2025 the parols were exhibited every evening from December 14 to January 1. Most nights were at Robinsons Starmills, but on some dates they were set up elsewhere: Capital Town Pampanga on December 19, MarQuee Mall in Angeles on December 27–28, and City Town Center in Calulut on December 29–30.

children.text: In 2025 there was a special exhibition at 9 p.m. on December 24 between San Fernando City Hall and the Metropolitan Cathedral. If you want to enjoy the Christmas Eve atmosphere, check that year's announcement.
According to a 2025 guide, visitors could watch for free. The only costs are food, drinks and transport, so it is an easy year-end family outing.
According to Wikipedia, 12 barangays took part in 2019, the most since 2006, and only 7 joined the 2020 exhibition. The number changes every year, so check the announcement for this year's scale.
Leave Manila. On competition day NLEX gets congested after 4 p.m., so it is best to set out early.
Arrive at Robinsons Starmills and park or get dropped off nearby. Many reviews say parking is extremely limited, so public transport is recommended.
Find your spot. There is a tip that the area slightly left of center, facing the front, has a wide view.
Have an early dinner. Restaurant lines get long between 4 and 6 p.m.
When the competition starts, watch each barangay's parol in turn. The start time differs each year, so check the latest announcement.
When the event ends, head home slowly to avoid the crowds, or stay overnight in Angeles or Clark.
Competition night is the most crowded, but the atmosphere is the best.
Explore central San Fernando in the afternoon. Heritage sites such as Bacolor Church and Betis Church are nearby.
Arrive 30–45 minutes before the exhibition starts to get a front spot.
Watch that day's exhibition. Turn off your flash when taking photos and hold your device low.
Have dinner at a nearby restaurant and head home.
Take NLEX from Manila to Clark or Angeles and drop off your bags.
Visit central San Fernando and Bacolor Church. The traces of the church buried by volcanic mudflow are striking.
Watch the exhibition or competition and stay overnight nearby.
Eat a Pampanga-style breakfast, stop by Betis Church or Mount Arayat, then return to Manila.
Staying overnight lets you avoid the crowded trip home and enjoy the year-end evening at a relaxed pace.
Take a northbound bus that passes through San Fernando from terminals such as Cubao in Quezon City, Pasay and Avenida in Manila.

Vehicles are scarce on competition night when heading home, so decide on your ride in advance.

The competition has usually been held around the second Saturday of December: December 14 in 2024 and December 13 in 2025. The exhibition continues from late December to January 1, so if you miss one night you still have a chance to see it again.
The exact schedule is announced each year by the city tourism office or on the official Facebook page and may change. Check the latest announcement before booking flights and lodging.
Year-end is the start of the Philippine dry season, so rain is less of a worry, but evenings can be breezy and cool, so bring a light jacket.

A day trip is possible, but the trip home after competition night is long, so staying overnight in San Fernando or in Angeles or Clark is more comfortable. Lodging prices rise at year-end, so book early.

Restaurants cluster around the venue at Robinsons Starmills and SM City Pampanga, but lines are long between 4 and 6 p.m. on competition day. Pampanga is called the culinary capital of the Philippines, so it is also a good chance to try local food.

In the year-end peak season, hotels in Clark and Angeles fill up quickly. Central San Fernando has fewer lodging options, so book early. Carry both cash and a card; water and snacks can be bought at shops in and around the venue.
On competition day, arrive between 2:30 and 3:30 p.m. to secure a spot.
During the exhibition period, arriving 30–45 minutes before the start is enough.
Bring a power bank, comfortable shoes and a light jacket.
Turn off your flash and hold your device low so you do not block the view of people behind you.
Reviews say the area slightly left of center at the front has a wide view.
With children or older travelers, the exhibition period is easier than competition day.
Decide on your transport home in advance.
Older information may list a different venue from today's, so check the venue in this year's announcement.
Results of the competition are posted by local media (such as SunStar Pampanga) the same night, so you can check them even if you cannot attend.
Parking and transport home are very congested on competition day, so plan on public transport and extra time.
The schedule and venue change from year to year, so always check the latest announcement.
Sparks from the rotating devices have been reported before, so do not get too close to the parols.
Crowds at night call for caution against pickpockets; keep valuables in front of you.
